paper.title_en: Gravitational-Wave Sky Mapping with Pulsar Timing Arrays: The Full Earth-Pulsar Response and Resolution Operational Regimes
paper.abstract_en: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are usually analyzed in the Earth-term approximation, although the exact response of an Earth--pulsar baseline contains additional angular structure through the pulsar term. We develop a tensor-spherical-harmonic framework for PTA sky mapping of a deterministic, band-limited gravitational-wave strain field, retaining the full Earth--pulsar response. The single-baseline response is reduced to a compact analytical closed form involving two spherical Bessel functions. Its asymptotic analysis reveals four regimes: Earth-term dominance, transition, pulsar-term dominance, and an effective diffraction cutoff at $l_\mathrm{cut}\simeqωL$. This scale characterizes the intrinsic exponential suppression of an individual baseline, while the practical angular resolution of a PTA is primarily governed by the finite number, sky distribution and timing noise of the pulsars. Formulating PTA sky mapping as a linear inverse problem; we derive the associated Fisher information matrix and construct an singular-value-decomposition-based reconstruction framework that explicitly separates observable and poorly constrained sky modes. The analysis clarifies the relationship between intrinsic detector resolution and array-sampling limitations and provides a quantitative assessment of the circumstances under which coherent pulsar-term information becomes relevant for full-sky reconstruction. Idealized scaling arguments suggest that exploiting the transition/pulsar-term-dominated regime in global sky mapping imposes a severe $\sim l^4$ penalty on the array size required to maintain uniform reconstruction fidelity at high multipoles. The formalism extends naturally to anisotropic stochastic backgrounds and provides a unified framework for deterministic field reconstruction and angular-power anisotropy inference.
